10.section: The hippocampus keeps reading after the lights go out
10.role: Sets up study of hippocampal activity under anesthesia

propositions.claim: The older model of the brain assigns consciousness a central executive role in noticing, deciding, remembering, and explaining.
A newer view compares the brain to a building at night, where the front desk is closed but some departments keep working.
Seven epilepsy patients received propofol anesthesia during surgery.
Neuropixels probes were placed in these patients deep enough to record individual cells in the hippocampus.
A Nature paper reports the study.
The recording window was about ten to twenty minutes per patient.
Access to record from the hippocampus this way is rare.
The study asked what happens when speech and sound enter a brain whose owner will later remember none of it.

12.section: The hippocampus keeps reading after the lights go out
12.role: Summarizes hippocampal responses to sounds and speech under anesthesia

propositions.claim: In the experiment, patients first heard repeated tones that included occasional deviant (oddball) tones.
Hippocampal neurons adapted to the repeated tones.
The neurons learned the tone pattern well enough to flag the oddball tones as exceptions.
Patients were next played speech.
Hippocampal cells tracked the meanings of words.
Hippocampal cells tracked the grammatical roles of words.
Hippocampal cells tracked the probability of which word might come next.
Words with similar meanings produced related patterns of neural activity.
The patients were anesthetized.
The anesthetized patients remembered nothing from the speech stream.
Despite the lack of memory, the hippocampus still processed language in a structured way.
A Scientific American summary described the result as overheard words being processed under anesthesia without later recall.

14.section: The hippocampus keeps reading after the lights go out
14.role: Reframes anesthesia as loss of binding, not processing

propositions.claim: The view being proposed is more limited than the idea of hidden wakefulness under anesthesia.
Some brain regions may continue to process language while the system that makes experience belong to a person is inactive.
A sentence can be processed without being experienced as one's own.
The anesthesia case suggests something about the self.
Consciousness may be less the part that does the work than a layer that binds distributed processing into one remembered scene.
When the binding layer is shut off, processing can still continue.

16.section: A dream can spend the night on your behalf
16.role: Introduces hyperoneirism as exhausting epic dreaming

propositions.claim: Sleep is expected to be the period in which the body repairs itself.
Some dreams function more like a second job than like rest.
The episode discusses hyperoneirism, which is also called epic dreaming.
Hyperoneirism involves long, vivid, continuous dream experiences.
People with hyperoneirism feel exhausted after these dreams.
The exhaustion occurs even when standard sleep measures appear normal.
Patients report nights of dreams containing plots, missions, conversations, travel, conflict, and obligation.
Patients wake feeling as though they have already worked a shift.

18.section: A dream can spend the night on your behalf
18.role: Argues dreams reveal hidden physical costs of sleep

propositions.claim: A patient can have normal results on a sleep chart.
Breathing can appear normal on the chart.
Muscle activity can appear normal on the chart.
Sleep stages can appear normal on the chart.
Despite the normal chart, the patient can wake up with a physical cost from the night.
Medicine often runs into cases where a patient experiences a pattern before clinicians have a clean instrument to measure it.
In such cases, the patient's private report comes first, classification of the pattern comes afterward, and treatment comes after that.
Epic dreaming is significant because it makes a hidden layer of sleep costly.
During epic dreaming, the body spends the night inside a story, and the person's waking self inherits the result in the morning.

20.role: Presents daraxonrasib pancreatic cancer survival result

propositions.claim: The passage's medical-news section continues the same argument from perception to tissue.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is a disease where optimism has to be earned in small steps.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is often detected late.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma spreads fast.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has resisted many therapies that changed other cancers.
The daraxonrasib result had an unusually strong impact because of this context.

In the Phase 3 RASolute 302 trial in previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer, median overall survival was about 13.2 months with daraxonrasib.
In the same trial, median overall survival was about 6.7 months with standard chemotherapy.

Dana-Farber's clinical summary makes the same central point that this is a serious survival signal in a very hard disease.

22.role: Frames cancer as a control-system failure

propositions.claim: The claim about the treatment has two parts that both need to be stated.

The deeper lesson is about system architecture.
Cancer is a broken control system involving growth signals, DNA repair, immune evasion, tissue pressure, nutrient routes, local signaling, and evolutionary selection.
A drug matters when it reaches a control node.
A small molecule can change a map.

24.section: A tumor can change the neighborhood rules
24.role: Introduces tumor-driven elimination of neighboring cells

propositions.claim: Chromosomal instability is the condition of cells having abnormal chromosome numbers or structures.

The episode's next paper describes an additional territorial behavior of tumors.
Some chromosomally unstable tumor cells enter a senescent-like state.

IRB Barcelona's study summary describes the work as a fruit-fly model in which tumors clear room around themselves.

26.section: A tumor can change the neighborhood rules
26.role: Explains how senescent cells aid tumors

propositions.claim: A senescent cell is expected to stop dividing.

28.section: A tumor can change the neighborhood rules

propositions.claim: The supporting evidence comes from experiments on fruit flies.

30.section: A tiny gland can lock a whole life state
30.role: Medical case illustrating hormonal control of fertility

propositions.claim: A woman has one child, stops breastfeeding, and then develops secondary infertility.
After she stopped breastfeeding, her body kept producing milk.
She also has headaches, night sweats, and fatigue.
Prolactin is a hormone that helps drive lactation.
Excess prolactin can suppress ovulation.
The source of the excess prolactin is a pituitary tumor at the base of the brain.
When the tumor is removed, prolactin returns to normal levels and pregnancy becomes possible again.
The case takes up little screen time, but it illustrates a control system well.
A tiny gland can set a reproductive state affecting the whole body.
A signal for lactation can act as a lock on fertility.
A local mass can become a problem that affects the course of a person's life.
Bodies have dashboards, but people mostly experience only the output.

32.section: Repair may be a locked program
32.role: Introduces spinal-cord section and the Cell Reports study

34.role: Cautions and hopeful framing about lynestrenol finding

propositions.claim: Lynestrenol is a synthetic progestin used as a contraceptive.

36.role: Summarizes episode theme: hidden control layers precede conscious self

propositions.claim: The episode is a digest that moves across many topics: a haunted lab, infrasound, anesthesia, dreams, pancreatic cancer, tumor ecology, prolactin, and spinal repair.
The common thread across these topics is a hidden control layer.
Vibration can alter stress before it is perceived as sound.
The hippocampus processes language before memory receives a scene.
A dream uses up the night before the waking self can object to it.
A cancer cell changes the rules governing tissue.
A pituitary signal suppresses reproduction.

Most of the body runs on older regulatory machinery: sensors, thresholds, switches, chemical signals, emergency policies, developmental locks, local negotiations, and inherited evolutionary leftovers that still operate.
Consciousness remains part of the picture and becomes more interesting, as the layer that makes a world reportable after deeper systems have already acted.
A person is a layered organism, and many layers are already processing information before the conscious person arrives.
